newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Talks between S-E-Banken/Nordbanken hit wall.
newsitem.headline: Talks between S-E-Banken/Nordbanken hit wall.

text.p: Swedish commercial bank S-E-Banken and state-controlled Nordbanken surprised the market on Monday by announcing that talks widely expected to end in a merger had ended with no conclusion.
"Nordbanken and Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken have discussed a possible merger. These discussions have been brought to an end without result," the banks said in a statement.
Swedish banking shares have risen sharply since last autumn on rumours of a shake-up in the sector, widely seen to be over-supplied and ripe for mergers.
Swedish media reports had said a merger between S-E-Banken and Nordbanken, which is 59 percent state-owned, was imminent.
On Friday S-E-Banken shares were trading at 72.5 crowns and Nordbanken shares at 235 crowns, but the failure of the talks was expected to hit the market hard at the open at 0900 GMT.
"It will come as a bit of a surprise as expectations have been running at a high level," said banking analyst Keith Baird from Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
"It will disappoint many in the market. If you look at the run up in the Nordbanken share price it shows there was a lot of credibility given to this."
The end of merger talks left analysts uncertain about the government's next move.
However Finance Mininster Erik Asbrink said the state's holding in Nordbanken was still for sale but that there was no timetable set.
Some analysts said the merger between the two banks had raised doubts in some quarters over the revenues of a merged operation.

"We thought that this merger would decrease profits in the new bank compared to the two banks because of the decrease in revenues and because the competition between banks in Sweden is so strong," said Jonny Sylven, analyst at Swedbank.
"I think the end of the merger is good for Nordbanken but S-E-Banken will probably have some problems with a change in strategy now.
"I think that really both of them wanted to merge but they realise there is a lot of problems with revenue through this."
Nordbanken posted a nine month operating profit of 5.7 billion crowns ($783 million) in 1996, an increase of 13 percent over the same 1995 period.
In September 1996 Nordbanken proposed a five billion crown share buy-back which reduced the government's holding to 59.4 percent from 65.5 percent.
S-E-Banken posted an operating profit of 4.42 billion crowns for the first nine months of 1996 compared to 2.06 billion in the same 1995 period. ($ = 7.276 Swedish Crowns)
